w: A 1970s-revival cocktail terrace above the Park South Hotel, rattan chairs and potted palms framing an unbroken sweep of Midtown towers. Climb past the bar to the open-air deck at dusk and the Empire State Building turns pink through the haze while the avenues hum thirty storeys below.
s: 1970s-glam rooftop terrace over Midtown
why: A newly opened 2025 rooftop revives vintage New York glamour with sweeping Midtown skyline views.

w: One floor below Miralto in the Torre Latinoamericana, glass walls turn the whole compass: the Zocalo and cathedral towers to the east, Chapultepec's forest to the west, and on a clear afternoon the twin volcanoes Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl on the horizon. The entire Centro Historico unrolls underfoot.
s: Four-cardinal-point views from a 1956 tower
why: A panoramic bar atop Latin America's first skyscraper, overlooking the historic centre and volcanoes.

w: The highest point in Stanley Park drops away in a sheer bluff above First Narrows, the Lions Gate Bridge slung low across the water and the North Shore mountains rising behind it. Cargo ships idle in English Bay, cormorants nest in the cliff face below, and old-growth forest presses right up to the railing.
s: Cliff-edge lookout over Lions Gate Bridge
why: Stanley Park's signature bluff view of bridge, harbour and mountains, framed by old-growth forest.

w: A residential dead-end above the Don Valley opens onto the Prince Edward Viaduct striding across the ravine, the CN Tower needling up beyond a jumble of downtown glass. Locals bring folding chairs at sunset; there is no railing, no sign and no ticket booth, just a gap in the hedge and the whole skyline.
s: Unmarked dead-end with a full skyline view
why: A residential-street secret giving one of Toronto's best unobstructed views of the viaduct and skyline.

w: Thirty-nine floors up in the Marriott Marquis, arched windows wrap the room in a full circuit of the bay: the Bay Bridge strung with lights on one side, Alcatraz a dark smudge on the water, fog sometimes pouring over Twin Peaks like a slow tide rolling in from the west. Order a drink and just walk the loop.
s: 360-degree bay views from arched windows
why: One of SoMa's highest bars, giving a full circular sweep of San Francisco Bay from Alcatraz to the bridge.

w: A funicular and cable car climb to the white sanctuary crowning the ridge at 3,152 metres above Bogota, and from the terrace the Andean capital spreads out in a haze of red brick and traffic, the savanna running to a rim of far-off green mountains. Pilgrims still climb the old stone path on their knees.
s: Andean sanctuary above the whole savanna
why: The pilgrimage hill that gives Bogota's most complete panorama, reached by funicular or cable car since 1929.

w: The fire-gutted shell of a Belle Epoque mansion is left standing as a public terrace, steel walkways threaded through roofless brick rooms once filled with early-1900s artists. Climb the tower stair and Guanabara Bay opens out below, Sugarloaf and the Lapa Arches laid flat beneath the tram tracks.
s: Burnt-out mansion turned bay-view terrace
why: A ruined Belle Epoque salon in Santa Teresa converted into a free public lookout over Guanabara Bay.

w: Concrete gun emplacements from a Civil War anti-aircraft battery still ring the summit, scrawled with layers of graffiti and crowded most evenings with people passing around bottles of cava. Below, the whole Eixample grid runs out to Sagrada Familia's spires and the flat blue line of the Mediterranean beyond.
s: Wartime bunkers turned sunset picnic spot
why: A former Civil War flak battery, now Barcelona's favourite unofficial sunset lookout over the whole grid.

w: A quarter-scale iron echo of the Eiffel Tower rises from a wooded hilltop above the Vltava, reached by funicular through orchards and a rose garden. Climb the 299 steps and Prague's red roofs and hundred spires spread out below, Prague Castle close enough to see the changing of the guard through binoculars.
s: Mini Eiffel Tower over a hundred spires
why: An 1891 lookout tower on a funicular-topped hill, giving Prague's widest rooftop-and-spire panorama.

w: The highest of Lisbon's viewpoints sits above a small whitewashed chapel, with no cafe and no crowds of tour groups to block the view. Castelo de Sao Jorge and the Tagus estuary spread out below in a jumble of terracotta roofs, and the sunset here turns the whole river into a sheet of hammered copper.
s: Lisbon's highest lookout, chapel included
why: The highest of the Graca miradouros, favoured by locals for sunsets over the castle and the Tagus.

w: Seven fairy-tale turrets, one for each Magyar tribe that settled the Carpathian basin, line a neo-Romanesque terrace built where medieval fishermen once defended the riverbank. Between the arches the Danube unrolls south past the Chain Bridge to Parliament's spires on the Pest side, best caught floodlit after dark.
s: Seven turrets over the Danube and Chain Bridge
why: A fantasy-castle terrace on Castle Hill giving Budapest's classic postcard view of Parliament and the Danube.

w: A funicular burrows through the limestone to the highest point in central Athens, where a whitewashed chapel and an open-air theatre share the summit with a terrace bar. The Acropolis floats below among a sea of low apartment blocks, and on clear evenings the view carries to the Saronic Gulf.
s: Funicular summit above the Acropolis
why: Athens' highest hill, reached by a rock-tunnel funicular, gives the widest rooftop view over the whole basin.

w: A squat 13th-century gate tower in the Upper Town fires a cannon at noon exactly as it has since 1877, deafening anyone on the narrow gallery beneath it. The climb up a tight spiral stair rewards with red rooftops of Gornji Grad in the foreground and Medvednica's forested ridge filling the northern skyline.
s: Medieval tower with a noon cannon blast
why: A 13th-century defence tower whose noonday cannon and rooftop gallery are a Zagreb daily ritual.

w: A glass-edged timber platform cantilevers out from the mountainside 650 metres above Aurlandsfjord, nothing on the glass lip to break the drop to the water. The fjord runs turquoise-blue between sheer walls toward Flam, and in winter the platform sits above the clouds while snow buries the road behind it.
s: Glass-edged platform 650m above a fjord
why: A cantilevered glass viewpoint on the Snow Road, one of the most photographed fjord overlooks in Norway.

w: A rooftop inside a 19th-century apartment block on Istiklal Street opens onto a full 360-degree circuit of the old city: minarets of the Suleymaniye and Blue Mosque needling the skyline south, the Bosphorus glinting between the hills, the Golden Horn's bridges strung with lights as the call to prayer rises.
s: Full-circle rooftop over minarets and strait
why: A landmark Istiklal Street rooftop that turns a full circle over the old city, the Bosphorus and Golden Horn.

w: Perched above the old grain silo turned Zeitz museum, this terrace lines up Table Mountain's flat summit dead ahead across the harbour, with tankers and yachts working the water below and Robben Island a low shape out in Table Bay. The cloth of cloud, when it comes, rolls over the mountain in slow motion.
s: Silo-top terrace facing Table Mountain
why: A converted grain silo's rooftop bar with an unbroken view of Table Mountain across the working harbour.

w: Chains bolted into the rock haul hikers up the final scramble to a summit that gives the one view Table Mountain cannot give itself: Table Mountain whole, flat-topped and immense, City Bowl spilling down one side, Camps Bay's white sand curling round the other. Full-moon hikers queue with headlamps for the ascent.
s: Chain-assisted scramble facing Table Mountain
why: Cape Town's favourite sunset and full-moon summit, giving the classic head-on view of Table Mountain.

w: A lattice-concrete tower shaped like a lotus flower rises from an island in the Nile, its restaurant turning slowly through a full circle each hour. West, over the river's braided channels, the Giza pyramids sit hazy on the desert edge; east, minarets crowd the Citadel and Islamic Cairo's rooftops.
s: Lotus-shaped tower over the Nile and pyramids
why: Cairo's tallest structure, a 1961 lotus-form tower that on clear days lines up the Nile with the Giza pyramids.

w: The only rooftop bar in the world that looks straight into a national park: past the pool's edge, the acacia scrub of Nairobi National Park runs unbroken to a horizon where giraffe and zebra sometimes graze in silhouette against the city's distant towers. Sundowners here come with actual wildlife, not just a skyline.
s: Sundowners facing wild giraffe and zebra
why: A hotel rooftop bar directly overlooking Nairobi National Park, unique among city sundowner spots worldwide.

w: Sixty-two floors above the Corniche, floor-to-ceiling glass wraps a full circuit of the Gulf: dhows and tankers working the water, the white domes of Sheikh Zayed Mosque glowing across the bay, and Saadiyat Island's museums a low line on the horizon. At night the whole waterfront ignites in a strip of gold light.
s: Gulf views over dhows and a floodlit mosque
why: One of the highest bars in Abu Dhabi, with a rare unobstructed sightline to the floodlit Sheikh Zayed Mosque.

w: A cable car swings up from Rike Park to the base of a 20-metre aluminium statue of a woman holding a sword in one hand and a wine bowl in the other, Tbilisi's guardian since 1958. From her plinth the old town's tin roofs and sulphur bathhouse domes sit beneath the snow line of the Caucasus.
s: Sword-and-wine statue above the old town
why: Tbilisi's guardian statue on Sololaki Hill, reached by cable car, overlooks the old town toward the Caucasus.

w: Glass elevators haul visitors to the 118th floor of the world's second-tallest building, where a rotating Bubble Tram completes a slow lap outside the sealed observation hall. The Petronas Towers, once the tallest thing in the skyline, now look small against the Klang River basin and green hills.
s: Bubble Tram atop the world's 2nd-tallest tower
why: A 2024-opened deck on the world's second-tallest building, with a rotating rooftop tram unique among sky decks.

w: A free viewing floor on the 46th storey of an office and shopping complex gets almost none of the queues that clog Tokyo's paid towers, so the wraparound windows are often nearly empty. It faces Tokyo Bay and Odaiba's ferris wheel instead of the usual skyline, Rainbow Bridge tracing a curve of light after dark.
s: Free 46th-floor deck facing Tokyo Bay
why: A little-known free observation floor overlooking Tokyo Bay and Odaiba, overlooked by most sightseers.

w: Sixty-three floors above the financial district, a star-shaped light installation hangs over a terrace that claims the highest rooftop bar in Singapore. The Marina Bay skyline crowds one side, container ships queue at anchor in the strait on the other, and the river threads a dark line through the CBD towers below.
s: Star-lit terrace over the CBD and strait
why: Singapore's highest rooftop bar, 282 metres up, with sightlines across Marina Bay and the shipping strait.

w: The 65th floor of the Lotte Center puts Hanoi's Old Quarter, West Lake and Truc Bach Lake all in the same frame, the Red River curling around paddy fields beyond the last apartment blocks. On hazy days the horizon dissolves into rice-green farmland; on clear ones the karst hills toward Ha Long Bay are just visible.
s: City's highest bar over two lakes
why: Hanoi's tallest rooftop bar, spanning views from the Old Quarter and West Lake out to the edge of farmland.

w: Terraced lawns and topiary hedges clipped into animal shapes sit on top of the city's main water reservoir, built in 1881 partly to screen the view from a nearby Parsi Tower of Silence. From the western edge the Arabian Sea opens out, and after dark the curve of Marine Drive below lights up as the Queen's Necklace.
s: Reservoir-top garden facing the Queen's Necklace
why: A Victorian reservoir garden atop Malabar Hill giving Mumbai's best view of the Marine Drive night lights.

w: On the 118th floor of the Ritz-Carlton inside the International Commerce Centre, glass walls put Hong Kong's skyline underfoot instead of at eye level: Victoria Harbour a thread of light, Victoria Peak a dark hump on the far shore, container ships crawling between islands lost in the evening haze below.
s: The world's highest bar, harbour underfoot
why: The highest bar in the world at 480 metres, looking straight down on Victoria Harbour and the Peak.

w: At the dead end of a bush road north of the city, sandstone cliffs drop to Pittwater and Broken Bay meeting the open Tasman Sea, Barrenjoey Lighthouse a white pin on the headland opposite. Whales pass close to the cliffline on their winter migration, and the bush around the lookout still smells of eucalyptus and salt.
s: Sandstone cliffs where two waterways meet
why: A national-park cliff lookout where Pittwater meets the open sea, a favourite for winter whale-watching.
